Juvenile Argentine croaker (Umbrina canosai) recruit to coastal nursery grounds following a pelagic larval phase that culminates in metamorphosis and benthic settlement. The onset of sexual maturation in this species is closely tied to body size, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of 15.9 cm [Lp = 15.9 cm]. This length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 44.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 44.7 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship validated for populations of the southwestern Atlantic. The transition from an immature to a reproductively capable adult involves a period of accelerated somatic growth, during which substantial lipid reserves are accumulated to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis. Field surveys conducted along the Uruguayan and Argentine continental shelf indicate that the age at which 50 percent of individuals reach this developmental milestone is closely tied to thermal regime. Data collected from fish held under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C] have provided insight into the physiological basis of this size threshold.

Measurements taken from gravid females during the peak of the spawning season yielded a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%], obtained from specimens maintained at 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C]. Histological examination of ovarian tissue has confirmed the presence of oocytes at various stages of vitellogenesis, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy.

The ultimate body size that an individual of this species can achieve is reflected in the maximum recorded total length, which has been documented at 53.3 cm [Li = 53.3 cm] from extensive sampling of the commercial fishery catch. This asymptotic length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 18,544 grams [Wwi = 18,544 grams] when the allometric length-weight conversion is applied, representing the largest adults observed in the population. Individuals approaching this maximum size are typically aged individuals that have experienced favorable feeding conditions over multiple years. The growth trajectory of Umbrina canosai is characterized by a rapid initial phase during the first few years of life, followed by a gradual deceleration as the fish approach their asymptotic length. Comparative life-history data from congeneric species such as Umbrina cirrosa suggest that the ultimate length of Argentine croaker is consistent with that of a medium-bodied sciaenid adapted to temperate continental shelf environments. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a positive allometric pattern, indicating that larger individuals become disproportionately heavier as they grow.

Hatching marks the beginning of the exogenous feeding phase for the yolk-sac larva, which emerges from the demersal egg after a brief incubation period. The wet weight at birth of Umbrina canosai is extraordinarily low, measured at just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], a value consistent with the small diameter of the pelagic egg, which measures approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter. This minuscule initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before it must commence active foraging on planktonic prey. The transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrition is a critical period of high mortality, as the feeding larva must successfully locate and capture suitably sized zooplankton to sustain rapid growth. The larval rearing environment, characterized by water temperatures of 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C], influences the rate of yolk absorption and the timing of mouth opening, both of which are crucial for survival through the first-feeding stage. Observations from laboratory rearing trials indicate that larval growth rates during this early phase are sensitive to even small fluctuations in thermal conditions.

The maximum documented lifespan of Argentine croaker in the wild, derived from otolith-based age estimates of the oldest individuals captured in research trawl surveys, reaches 26 years [am = 26 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C]. This longevity is relatively extended for a sciaenid of its body size and suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high annual reproductive output. The species exhibits a Type III survivorship curve, with extremely high mortality during the egg and larval stages giving way to much lower and relatively constant mortality among juveniles and adults. Management strategies for this commercially important species have therefore emphasized the need for size limits and seasonal closures that protect the spawning stock. Ongoing monitoring of age structure in the fishery is essential for the sustainable exploitation of this long-lived marine teleost.
